summary: Describes SRL, a language for writing rulesets, which are configuration files loaded into a traffic flow meter. The rules say which flows to measure and what information to store for each. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: SRL is a language for writing instruction files for a device that measures network traffic. A program is run once for every packet that passes, and its job is to decide whether the packet belongs to a flow worth counting, to remember which flow it is, and to add one to that flow's totals. The program may also be run a second time with the sender and receiver swapped, so that each flow is counted once with counters for both directions.

subtitle: A small configuration language for traffic meters: it says which flows to measure and what to record about each one.

tldr.problem: A traffic flow meter is configured with a ruleset, and writing one means writing machine code for the meter's matching engine. Most users find that confusing and difficult.
tldr.mechanism: SRL is a procedural language for writing those rulesets. A program is run from the beginning for every arriving packet, tests the packet's attributes, saves the values that identify the flow, and counts it. Programs are compiled into rulesets that are downloaded to the meter.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational. It describes the language and gives two worked examples, and points at a free implementation, the NeTraMet compiler, version 4.2.

today: RFC 2723 is an Informational memo from October 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a configuration language and points at a free implementation of it, the NeTraMet compiler, but the language itself is not a standard and nothing requires a meter to use it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A ruleset for an RTFM meter is a sequence of instructions to be executed by the meter's Pattern Matching Engine. The form of these instructions is described in detail in the RTFM Architecture and RTFM Meter MIB documents, but most users, at least initially, find them confusing and difficult to write, mainly because the effect of each instruction is strongly dependent on the state of the meter's Packet Matching Engine at the moment of its execution.

SRL, the Simple Ruleset Language, is a procedural language for creating RTFM rulesets. It has been designed to be simple for people to understand, using statements which help to clarify the execution context in which they operate. SRL programs are compiled into rulesets, which can then be downloaded to RTFM meters. An SRL compiler is available as part of NeTraMet, a free-software implementation of the RTFM meter and manager, version 4.2.

The RTFM Architecture defines a set of attributes that apply to network traffic. Among them are address attributes such as PeerType, PeerAddress, TransType and TransAddress, which have meaning for many protocols. For IPv4 traffic, PeerType is 1, PeerAddress is an IP address, TransType is TCP (6), UDP (17) or ICMP (1), and TransAddress is usually an IP port number.

An RTFM traffic flow is a stream of packets observed by a meter as they pass across a network between two end points, or to or from a single end point, and each end point of a flow is specified by the set of values of its address attributes. An RTFM meter is a measuring device, for example a program running on a Unix or PC host, which observes passing packets and builds flow data records for the flows of interest. RTFM traffic flows are bidirectional, so each flow data record in the meter has two sets of counters, one for packets travelling from source to destination and the other for returning packets.

A meter must be configured by the user, which means creating a ruleset that says which flows are to be measured and how much information, meaning which attributes, should be stored for each of them. In the past, creating a ruleset meant writing machine code for the Packet Matching Engine, which has proved rather difficult. SRL provides a high-level language that lets users create effective rulesets without understanding the details of the engine. The language may also be useful in other application areas, being suitable for any application which involves selecting traffic flows from a stream of packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic meter watches packets go past and keeps a table of the conversations it sees, with a count of packets and bytes for each. Deciding which conversations to record used to mean writing the meter's own machine code. SRL is an ordinary programming language for writing those instruction files instead, and a compiler turns them into the form the meter understands.

sections.title: SRL Overview
sections.content:
An SRL program is executed from the beginning for each new packet arriving at the meter. It has two essential goals. The first is to decide whether the current packet is part of a flow which is of interest and, if necessary, to determine its direction, that is, which of its end points is considered to be its source. Other packets will be ignored. The second is to save whatever information is required to identify the flow and to accumulate quantitative information for that flow.

At execution, the meter's Packet Matching Engine begins by using the source and destination attributes as they appear on the wire. If the attributes do not match those of a flow to be recorded, the engine will normally execute the program again, this time with the source and destination addresses interchanged. Because of this bidirectional matching, a meter is able to build up tables of flows with two sets of counters, one for forward packets and the other for backward packets. The programmer can, if required, suppress the reverse-direction matching and assign forward and backward directions that conform to the conventions of the external context.

The first goal is achieved using IF statements, which perform comparisons on information from the packet or from SRL variables. The second is achieved using one or more SAVE statements to store the flow's identification attributes, and a COUNT statement that increments the statistical data accumulating for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet starts the program again from the top. If the packet does not match anything, the engine runs the whole program again with the sender and receiver swapped, so a conversation is recognised whichever way round the packet happens to arrive. If that also fails, the packet is dropped. When a packet does match, the program notes down which values identify the conversation and then adds one to the counters.

sections.title: The Language: Tokens, Defines and Programs
sections.content:
The tokens of an SRL program obey a simple set of rules. Comments may appear on any line, following a hash sign. White space separates tokens. A semicolon terminates most statements. Identifiers, for example for defines and labels, must start with a letter, may contain letters, digits and underscores, and the case of letters is not significant. Reserved words, shown in capitals in the document, may not be used as identifiers. In the syntax diagrams keywords are written in capital letters, but in practice a compiler must be insensitive to case.

A program is a sequence of statements or declarations, with no special enclosing symbols. Statements and declarations terminate with a semicolon, except for compound statements, which terminate with a right brace. The only explicit declaration is the subroutine declaration; labels and subroutine parameters are declared implicitly.

The DEFINE directive gives a name to a piece of text. The syntax is DEFINE name = text;, where the text runs up to the closing semicolon. A semicolon inside the text must be preceded by a backslash, which in an SRL define produces a semicolon in the text. Wherever the name appears elsewhere in the program, it is replaced by the defined text. The memo's example defines the well-known port numbers and protocol numbers by name:

  • DEFINE ftp = (20, 21);
  • DEFINE telnet = 23;
  • DEFINE www = 80;

An IF statement evaluates a logical expression, and if the value is true it executes the action in the action part, which is either a SAVE action or another statement. If the value is false and the IF has an ELSE clause, that clause is executed; an ELSE clause always matches the immediately preceding IF, so a chain of ELSE IF statements gives a select-like structure. The simplest form of expression is a test for equality, in which an attribute value is masked and compared with a value. More complicated expressions are built with parentheses and the && and || operators.

Operand values may be written as dotted decimal, hexadecimal or as a character constant in apostrophes. Masks may be given as numbers, as dotted decimal such as &255.255, as hexadecimal such as &FF-FF, or as a width in bits such as /16. If a mask is not specified, an all-ones mask is used. A value is always combined with a mask, and the two together are called an operand, so 130.216.0.0 & 255.255.0.0 and 130.216/16 mean the same thing. A list of values in parentheses may also be given, and the test succeeds if the masked attribute equals any of them. Values are right-padded with zeroes, so the given numbers specify the leading bytes of masks and values. The operand values and masks must be consistent with the attribute being tested: a four-byte value is acceptable as a peer address but not as a transport address, which may not be longer than two bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Comments start with a hash sign, most statements end with a semicolon, and names are not case sensitive. The DEFINE directive gives a name to a piece of text that is then substituted wherever the name appears, which is how the examples keep their lists of port numbers in one place. The IF statement tests an attribute against a value, and the value can be given with a mask so that only part of it matters, for example the first two bytes of an address.

sections.title: The Statements
sections.content:
SAVE saves information which will later identify the flow in the meter's flow table. It does not actually record anything in the table; that is done when a subsequent COUNT statement executes. It has two forms. SAVE attrib = operand; saves the attribute, mask and value as given in the statement, which is useful because an imperative statement performs no test and so may save an arbitrary value. SAVE attrib; and SAVE attrib / width; save the attribute and mask from the statement together with the value resulting from applying them to the current packet, which is most useful when saving a value with a wider mask than was used to select the packet.

COUNT appears after all testing and saving is complete. It tells the engine to build the flow identifier from the attributes which have been saved, find it in the meter's flow table, creating a new entry if this is the first packet observed for that flow, and increment its counters. The meter then moves on to the next incoming packet.

IGNORE terminates examination of the current packet without saving anything from it, and the meter moves on to the next packet, beginning again at the first statement of the program. NOMATCH indicates that matching has failed for this execution of the program. If it is executed while the packet is being processed with its addresses in on-the-wire order, the engine performs the program again from the beginning with the source and destination addresses interchanged; if it is executed following such an interchange, the packet is ignored instead.

STORE assigns a value to an SRL variable and saves it. There are six SRL variables, named SourceClass, SourceKind, DestClass, DestKind, FlowClass and FlowKind. Their names have no particular significance, and they can be used to store any single-byte integer values. Their values are set to zero each time the examination of a new packet begins.

EXIT exits a labelled compound statement, so the next statement executed is the one following that compound statement. In practice the language provides enough logical structure that one seldom, if ever, needs it. RETURN is used to return from subroutines and is valid only inside one. A subroutine declaration names the subroutine, gives a parameter list in which each parameter is preceded by a keyword saying whether it is an SRL variable or any other RTFM attribute, and then the body, which is a sequence of statements terminated by the ENDSUB keyword. Exits in a subroutine may not refer to labels outside it, so the only way out is a RETURN statement. A CALL statement invokes a subroutine, and after the parameters comes a sequence of statements, each preceded by an integer label. A RETURN with a number jumps to the statement with that label in the calling statement; a RETURN without one continues with the statement immediately following ENDCALL. Execution of the labelled statement completes the CALL.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVE remembers which values identify the flow, without writing anything down yet. COUNT is what actually writes the entry and adds one to its counters. IGNORE throws a packet away. NOMATCH says the packet did not match and asks the engine to try again with the two addresses swapped. STORE puts a value in one of six scratch variables that the program can carry from one test to the next. EXIT jumps out of a labelled block, and RETURN leaves a subroutine.

sections.title: Two Example Programs
sections.content:
The first example classifies IP port numbers. It defines the address family number for IPv4, the well-known port numbers for ftp, telnet and www, and the protocol numbers for TCP and UDP. It then ignores anything that is not IPv4, and for TCP or UDP traffic it tests whether the source port is one of the well-known ones, using a NOMATCH action so that the well-known port ends up as the destination. The destination port then sets a kind marker: 'T' for telnet, 'W' for www, 'F' for ftp, and '?' for anything else. Finally it saves the source and destination peer addresses as 32-bit addresses and counts.

The second classifies traffic into groups of networks. It defines the author's own network and a list of other networks, then calls a subroutine named net_kind twice, once with the source address and once with the destination address, passing in a variable to receive the result. The subroutine checks whether the address is in the author's own network, in the list, or neither, saves the network address with a 16-bit or 24-bit mask accordingly, stores 10, 20 or 30 in the variable, and returns to a numbered label in the calling statement. The network numbers are held in the two DEFINE directives so they are easy to change.

A second version of the same program uses a NOMATCH statement so that the resulting flows have the author's own network as their source, which also rejects traffic from that network to itself. Traffic which has the author's network neither as source nor as destination has 24 bits of its peer addresses saved before being counted, even though the subroutine might only have saved 16.
sections.plainLanguage: The first program sorts traffic by what kind of service it uses, marking each flow with a letter for web, file transfer or telnet. The second sorts traffic by which network it belongs to, marking it with a number for the author's own network, for a list of other networks, or for everything else. The second one reuses a subroutine for both ends of the conversation, so the same test runs twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SRL is a language for creating rulesets, that is, configuration files, for RTFM traffic meters, and it does not present any security issues in itself.

On the other hand, flow data gathered using such rulesets may well be valuable, so it is important to take proper precautions to ensure that access to the meter and its data is secure. Ways to achieve this are discussed in detail in the Architecture and Meter MIB documents.

The memo's IANA section notes that its appendix lists the RTFM attributes by name together with the size in bytes of each attribute value, and that because SRL refers to attributes only by name, users do not have to know the attribute numbers. Allocating new attributes is covered in the RTFM Architecture document.
sections.plainLanguage: The language itself is harmless; it only writes configuration files. What matters is the data the meter collects, which can be sensitive, so the meter and its readings need to be protected. The memo also explains that the appendices list the attributes by name and size so that a person writing a ruleset does not have to look up any numbers.

items.title: SAVE
items.text: Remembers the values that identify the flow; writes nothing yet.

items.title: COUNT
items.text: Builds the flow identifier, finds or creates the entry, and adds one.

items.title: IGNORE
items.text: Throws the current packet away and moves to the next one.

items.title: NOMATCH
items.text: Says the match failed, so the program runs again with the addresses swapped.

items.title: STORE
items.text: Puts a value in one of the six scratch variables.

items.title: EXIT
items.text: Leaves a labelled compound statement early.

items.title: RETURN
items.text: Leaves a subroutine, optionally to a numbered label in the caller.
